All figures are expressed in 2024 USD unless otherwise noted. I use the discounted cash flow (DCF) approach with a 4 % annual discount rate—typical for employer‑sponsored plans—to compute net present value (NPV).  

**Drug Acquisition Costs**  
The average net price of a GLP‑1 agent after rebates is modeled at **$12,000 per patient per year**. This figure reflects the wholesale acquisition cost (WAC) of semaglutide or tirzepatide (~$15 k/month list price) minus an estimated 30 % rebate that insurers have historically secured for obesity indications.  
Assuming a conservative uptake of **300 patients** (≈6 % of the workforce, based on a 30 % obesity prevalence and a 20 % treatment‑eligible subset), the annual drug cost is:  

\[
300 \text{ patients} \times \$12{,}000/\text{patient/yr}= \$3{,}600{,}000.
\]

Over two years this becomes **$7.2 million** (no discounting applied yet).  

**Utilization‑Management Expenses**  
Prior authorization, quarterly monitoring visits, laboratory testing for HbA1c and lipid panels, and pharmacy coordination typically add about **$200 per patient per year** in administrative overhead. For 300 patients this equals:  

\[
300 \times \$200 = \$60{,}000/\text{yr},
\]

Additionally, improved weight status typically reduces absenteeism by about 10 %, which for a salaried worker translates to roughly **$500 in productivity gains** annually.  

Thus, the combined annual savings per treated patient are:  

\[

\]

For 300 patients this equals **$450 k per year**, or **$900 k over two years**.

      \approx \$6{,}420{,}000.

In other words, under these assumptions the employer would spend roughly **$6.4 million** more than it saves over two years by covering GLP‑1 agents for obesity.
